# Notes Before the Joint Session

*Written before the three functions are in the same room, deliberately. A plan assembled after that meeting will be a treaty. Treaties preserve borders, and the borders are the problem.*

---

## The number I don't believe yet

Fourteen weeks is not a duration. It's a promise, and promises contain padding, and padding is put there by people who have been burned. Somewhere inside the fourteen there is an amount of actual work — cutting, welding, machining, assembling, testing, measuring — and my working assumption, offered as an assumption rather than a finding, is that it's somewhere between eight and fifteen working days. Everything else is waiting.

That distinction is the whole plan. If most of the fourteen weeks is work, we have a capacity problem, and it costs capital to fix. If most of it is waiting, we have a queue problem, and queue problems are largely free to fix and are being defended by people who sincerely believe they're defending quality. I don't yet know which we have. I'd want to know before anyone proposes anything, including me.

The related thing I don't believe is the six. A competitor quoting six weeks is very probably not building faster. More likely they are quoting a narrower configuration envelope, holding the long-lead core on their own balance sheet, counting from a different event, or hitting the six about seventy percent of the time and absorbing the rest in goodwill. Any of those is a different response from us. It would be worth someone finding out which — ideally by asking two customers we lost rather than by asking the salesperson who lost them.

---

## An unhelpfully useful piece of evidence

"One in three deals lost on delivery alone" is a self-reported loss reason from the function that is graded on wins. That isn't a slur; it's how the world works. Loss reasons collected from sellers cluster on the causes the seller couldn't control. Nobody writes "lost on my failure to reach the specifier early."

I'd take it seriously anyway, because it's directionally plausible and because arguing about it costs us the room. But I'd want the version of it that comes from outside: a short set of calls to lost prospects, made by someone who isn't the account owner, asking what date they actually needed and what they did instead. My quiet suspicion is that we'll find two different losses wearing the same coat — some genuinely wanted six weeks, and some wanted a date they could *believe*, and we lost those on reliability rather than speed. Those two require opposite fixes. Speed for the first. Truthfulness and buffer for the second.

---

## What the warranty episode actually taught us, versus what we learned from it

The organisation's memory is "we compressed the schedule and quality broke." That memory is doing damage now, because it makes queue time and quality feel like the same substance, and it hands Quality a reason to treat every minute of waiting as a minute of protection.

I'd put a gentler reading on the record and see whether it survives contact with the files. What most likely happened was not that inspections were shortened. It was that under end-of-period pressure, units that failed something were kept moving — concessions granted, deviations signed, rework verification done in parallel with shipping paperwork, a witness point waived because the witness couldn't be got, and a handful of judgement calls made by tired people at eight in the evening on the last Friday of a quarter. The gates weren't removed. They were held open with a foot.

If that's roughly right, then the lesson is precise and quite different from the one we drew: **you can remove waiting without touching a gate, and you can destroy a product without removing a single gate at all.** Compressing an unchanged process by applying deadline pressure is the failure mode. Removing the reasons the process contains waiting is not the same act, and it's worth spending some effort making sure the room can hear the difference, because the entire plan lives in that gap.

The tell we'd watch, from week one, is the concession and deviation rate. It is the leading indicator we already had and didn't read. It rises before warranty claims do, by roughly the length of the warranty period.

---

## Where I'd expect the time to actually be

Offered as hypotheses in the order I'd test them, not as conclusions. Somebody should be walking real orders with a clipboard while this is being discussed.

**Before anything is ordered.** The stretch between purchase order and engineering release is, in businesses shaped like this one, frequently three to five weeks and almost never in anybody's lead-time model, because it's nobody's department. Spec clarification, customer approval drawings going out and coming back, a credit check, a deposit, an incomplete PO, a configuration nobody has built before requiring a decision from an engineer who's on holiday. The clock is running and the shop hasn't been told.

**The single longest-lead purchased item.** One casting, one gearbox, one pressure part, one control panel with an eleven-week quote sets the floor for everything, and if we place it at order entry rather than on forecast, we have chosen fourteen weeks in a single procurement habit.

**Queue in front of shared resources.** The machining centre, the paint booth, the test bay — and, I'd guess most importantly, the inspector. Time *under* inspection is short. Time *waiting for* inspection is where the certified process gets blamed for something it isn't doing.

**Third-party and witness scheduling.** External witness points booked when the part is ready rather than when the part is forecast. A two-day inspection that arrives eleven days after readiness.

**The rework loop nobody counts.** First-pass yield at each stage, and the invisible reappearance of work at the back of the queue it just left. This is the item where speed and quality genuinely are the same project rather than opponents.

**Batch and calendar artefacts.** Weekly order release, monthly build slots, campaign painting, ERP planning parameters set in 2011 by someone who has left, order-dispatch rules that reward the machine's utilisation rather than the order's progress.

**The dossier.** Finished machine, complete and correct, sitting on the floor while certificates, material traceability, and test reports are assembled by one person who does it at month end. I've seen a fortnight live here, and it's the least defensible fortnight in the building.

---

## Moves, grouped by the bet each one makes

I'd float these rather than propose them, and I'd be interested in which function reaches for which unprompted.

**1. Split the promise — a bet on segmentation rather than on the factory.**
One quoted lead time for everything means the fourteen weeks is set by our hardest order. A defined configuration envelope — the options that cover, say, seventy percent of volume — quoted at six or seven, with genuine engineered work quoted honestly at fourteen or sixteen, wins most of what we're losing without asking the shop to do anything heroic. The hard part is not operations. It's writing the boundary of that envelope down in a form Sales cannot quietly widen, and being willing to lose the deals outside it on purpose.

**2. Move the decoupling point — a bet on the balance sheet, dressed as an operations plan.**
Hold the long-lead common core in a generic, undifferentiated state and differentiate late. This is the single highest-leverage move available and it isn't really an operations decision at all; it's a decision to convert cash into calendar. One in three deals is the number to hold up when Finance asks what the carrying cost buys. Worth being honest that this is where the real argument is, and that it will be conducted in the language of inventory turns by people who have never lost a deal.

**3. Reduce variety in the long-lead items only — a bet on product architecture, slow and structural.**
Not a rationalisation programme. A narrow question: which three or four purchased items set our floor, and how few variants of those can cover most orders? This is unglamorous, takes eighteen months, and is the only one of these moves a competitor can't answer inside a year. Which is the usual signal that it's the one worth doing.

**4. Attack queue, cap work in progress — a bet that will feel like going backwards.**
Fewer orders on the floor at once move faster, individually and in total. The implication is a deliberate reduction in apparent utilisation and protective slack — perhaps fifteen to twenty percent — at the constraint. Production's scorecard currently punishes exactly this. Anyone who proposes it without first proposing to change that scorecard is asking someone to volunteer for a bad review.

**5. Treat inspection as a flow resource rather than a checkpoint — a bet that Quality is the ally, not the obstacle.**
No gate removed. Not one. Instead: staff inspection to the queue rather than to the average load, which probably means adding an inspector, which is cheap against a lost order. Move measurement to the station — on-machine probing, certified operator self-inspection with audit sampling, statistical process control feeding the gate — so that the certified hold point becomes a *confirmation* of something already known rather than the moment of discovery. Pre-book external witness slots against forecast and pay for the occasional wasted slot. Build the certification dossier continuously, in parallel, so it completes when the machine does. Every one of these makes the gate faster without making it weaker, and several of them make it stronger, which is the argument I'd actually lead with in front of Quality.

**6. Buy slots, not parts — a bet on supplier relationships as schedule.**
Blanket orders with capacity reservation and pull release on the two or three items that set the floor. Dual-source the worst of them. Source inspection or supplier certification to eliminate incoming inspection queue outright. We are currently asking suppliers to be fast on demand; better to pay them modestly to be available on schedule.

**7. Front-load the order — a bet that the cheapest weeks are the ones before we start.**
A configurator at order entry. Pre-approved standard drawing sets so the customer approval cycle disappears for envelope orders. A release rule with teeth: nothing enters the shop unreleased, and release is measured in days from PO. This costs almost nothing and may be a third of the win.

**8. Sell reliability, held loosely, because it will sound like an excuse.**
Eight weeks hit ninety-five percent of the time beats six weeks hit seventy. Some customers know this and are not being offered it by anyone. Worth two propositions and no more — it's a hedge, not a strategy, and it's the kind of idea that expands to fill whatever attention it's given, particularly among people who'd prefer not to change the factory.

---

## The constraint I'd design from, not to

Start from the gate list. Write down every certified hold point, what it catches, who is qualified to perform it, and what evidence it produces. Sign it once, early, quietly. Then put it outside the programme's authority entirely — an external condition of the work rather than a topic within it. Because a condition gets engineered around, whereas a topic gets re-opened at eight in the evening on the last Friday of a quarter by someone with a shipment and a good reason.

Everything on that list is untouchable. Everything *between* the items on that list is fair game, and it's where I'd expect to find most of the fourteen weeks.

Two things somebody should own from week one rather than discover in month nine:

First-pass yield per stage, measured now, before we change anything, so that we own a baseline nobody can dispute later. Speed applied to a process with poor first-pass yield doesn't produce speed. It produces the last two years again.

The concession and deviation rate, published weekly to all three functions. This is the programme's own tripwire, and I'd want it written before the evidence arrives: if concessions rise above baseline, the lead-time work pauses itself, automatically, without a meeting. Handing Quality a pre-agreed veto trigger is what buys their agreement to stop using queue time as a substitute for one.

---

## On the three functions

I'd rather not spend effort reconciling the three narratives. They're all true, which is why the argument is unresolvable, and each function is behaving correctly given how it is graded.

Production is measured on utilisation and absorption, so it batches, keeps the floor full, and treats work in progress as evidence of health. Quality is measured on escapes and never on cycle time, so waiting is free to them and caution is costless. Sales is measured on bookings, so it promises what wins and passes the consequence downstream. Nobody is being unreasonable. The scorecard is being unreasonable, through three people.

So I'd change the measurement rather than the attitudes, and I'd do it in the least interesting way possible: one shared set of three numbers that all three functions carry jointly — total order-to-ship lead time, delivery reliability against promise, and first-pass yield. No function owns one of them. Each is graded on all three. It's a slightly blunt instrument and it works, mostly because it makes the current arguments pointless rather than resolved.

Two things I'd do rather than say.

Walk twenty completed orders with timestamps, and have one person from each of the three functions do the walking together. Not a workshop. A physical walk with a clipboard, at the pace of the material. Time-stamped facts are difficult to argue with and, more usefully, they're difficult to argue with *in front of the person who walked beside you*. My expectation is that by the third order the blame conversation stops on its own, because the waiting turns out to belong to nobody, which means it belongs to all of them.

Then put the real disagreement in the room on purpose. Take the inventory proposal — the number, the actual cash — to Finance and Sales in the same week, and watch how it resolves. If that conversation is frictionless, we've learned nothing about whether anyone will defend this when the quarter gets tight. I'd want the argument early, when it's cheap, rather than in month nine when it arrives as a budget refusal.

A small seconded team, co-located, drawn on merit rather than seniority, led by someone without a functional stake in the answer. One thing I would ask upward for, once, quietly: cover for the inventory position and for the automatic-pause tripwire. Both are promises that only mean something if they were made above the level that will later want to break them.

---

## What I'd do first

Not a programme. Two measurements and one deliberately over-reaching experiment.

The twenty-order walk, producing touch time as a percentage of elapsed time, stage by stage. That single ratio determines which of the moves above are relevant and which are theatre.

A pathfinder order: one real machine, standard configuration, pulled through with unlimited attention, every queue jumped, every gate fully honoured, nothing waived, every hour logged. It tells us the floor of what the current system can do when the system isn't in the way. The gap between that number and fourteen weeks is the size of the prize, and it's a number, and numbers travel better between feuding functions than arguments do.

And no external announcement of anything. The quoted lead time stays at fourteen until we have hit the new one internally, repeatedly, without a rising concession rate. Announcing first and hoping the system catches up is precisely how the last attempt happened.

---
